summary: Looks at data flows in low-power and lossy networks that use RPL for routing, and lists the cases that require the RPL Packet Information option, the source routing header, and IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation. It aims to clarify when each is needed in the data plane.

plainLanguage.summary: RPL is the routing protocol used in low-power sensor networks. It marks every packet with extra headers that say which way the packet should go and how far it has come. RFC 9008 works out, case by case, which of those headers are actually needed, so that devices do not waste battery on them, and changes one header number so that a packet leaving the network is not thrown away by a router that does not understand it.

questions: when is rpl rpi option required
what is the rpl rpi option
when is ipv6 in ipv6 encapsulation needed in rpl
what is rpl storing mode versus non-storing mode
subtitle: When RPL packets need the RPI option, a source routing header, or IPv6-in-IPv6 wrapping, and a new RPI option type.

tldr.problem: RPL adds routing information to every data packet, and different parts of the network need different amounts of it. Implementers disagreed about when the RPL artifacts were needed, and the old RPL Option type made any packet carrying it get dropped by routers outside the network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9008 works through 24 data-plane use cases and states when the RPL Option, the RPL Source Route Header and IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation are each required. It also changes the RPL Option type from 0x63 to 0x23, so that a node which does not recognise the option skips it instead of discarding the packet.
tldr.outcome: The data plane rules become unambiguous, and a packet can leave the low-power network without being dropped by the first core router that meets it. A configuration flag lets a network move to the new option type without a flag day. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9008 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2021, and it has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 6553 and works with RFC 6550 and RFC 8138, and it is the reference for the RPI Option Type 0x23.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RPL, the IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks, is a routing protocol for constrained networks. RFC 6553 defines the RPL Option carried within the IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options header, which carries the RPLInstanceID and quickly identifies inconsistencies, that is loops, in the routing topology. The RPL Option is commonly referred to as the RPL Packet Information, although the RPI is the routing information defined in RFC 6550 and transported in the RPL Option. RFC 6554 defines the RPL Source Route Header, an IPv6 extension header to deliver datagrams within a RPL routing domain, particularly in Non-Storing mode.

These items are referred to as RPL artifacts, and they are seen on all of the data plane traffic that occurs in RPL-routed networks. They do not, in general, appear on the RPL control plane at all, which is mostly hop-by-hop traffic, with one exception being Destination Advertisement Object messages in Non-Storing mode.

It has become clear from attempts at multi-vendor interoperability, and from a desire to compress as many of the artifacts as possible, that not all implementers agree when artifacts are necessary, when they can be safely omitted, or removed. The ROLL Working Group analyzed how the IPv6 rules of RFC 2460 apply to the Storing and Non-Storing use of RPL, and the result was 24 data-plane use cases, exhaustively outlined in the document. During the processing of this document, new rules were published as RFC 8200, and this document was updated to reflect the normative changes in that document.

This document updates RFC 6553, changing the value of the Option Type of the RPL Option to make routers compliant with RFC 8200 ignore this option when it is not recognized. RFC 8138 defines a mechanism for compressing RPL Option information and the RH3 routing header type, as well as an efficient IPv6-in-IPv6 technique.

Most of the use cases described require IPv6-in-IPv6 packet encapsulation. When encapsulating and decapsulating packets, RFC 6040 must be applied to map the setting of the explicit congestion notification field between the inner and outer headers. Unconstrained uses of RPL are not in scope of this document, and applicability statements for those uses may provide different advice.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things travel with an RPL data packet: the RPL Option, a source route header, and sometimes an extra IPv6 header around the packet. Each costs bytes, and bytes cost battery. The document works out which of them each kind of traffic actually needs.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
A Routing Header is consumed when the Segments Left field is zero, which indicates that the destination in the IPv6 header is the final destination of the packet and that the hops in the Routing Header have been traversed.

A RPL leaf is an IPv6 host attached to a RPL router that obtains connectivity through a RPL Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graph. As an IPv6 node a RPL leaf is expected to ignore a consumed Routing Header, and as an IPv6 host it is expected to ignore a Hop-by-Hop Options header, so it can correctly receive a packet with RPL artifacts. It is not, however, expected to generate RPL artifacts or to support IP-in-IP encapsulation.

A RPL-Aware Node is a device that implements RPL, and it can be found inside or outside the low-power network. A RPL-Aware Leaf is a RPL-aware node that is also a RPL leaf. A RPL-Unaware Node is a device that does not implement RPL, and a RPL-Unaware Leaf is a RPL-unaware node that is also a RPL leaf.

A 6LoWPAN node is any host or router participating in a LoWPAN; in this document a 6LoWPAN node acts as a leaf. A 6LoWPAN router is an intermediate router in the LoWPAN that can send and receive Router Advertisements and Router Solicitations as well as forward and route IPv6 packets, and is present only in route-over topologies. A 6LoWPAN border router is located at the junction of separate 6LoWPAN networks, or between a 6LoWPAN network and another IP network; there may be more than one at the boundary, and the border router is the responsible authority for IPv6 prefix propagation for the network it serves.

A flag day is caused when a network is reconfigured in a way that nodes running the older configuration cannot communicate with nodes running the new configuration, the example given being the ARPANET's change from IP version 3 to IP version 4 on January 1, 1983. In the context of this document, a switch from RPI Option Type 0x63 to Option Type 0x23 presents as a disruptive changeover.

Non-Storing Mode is a RPL mode of operation in which the RPL-aware nodes send information to the root about their parents, so the root knows the topology. Because the root knows the topology, the intermediate routers do not maintain routing state, and source routing is needed. Storing Mode is a RPL mode of operation in which RPL-aware nodes maintain routing state for their children, so source routing is not needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of leaf matter. One speaks RPL; the other is a plain device that gets its connectivity through the RPL network without knowing anything about RPL. The second kind is the awkward one, because a packet addressed to it must not carry headers it will choke on.

sections.title: RPL Overview
sections.content:
RPL defines the RPL control message, which is an ICMPv6 message with a Type of 155. The DIS, DIO and DAO messages are all RPL control messages but with different Code values. The RPL stack sits above ICMPv6, which sits above IPv6, which sits above 6LoWPAN, which sits above the physical and MAC layers.

RPL supports two modes of downward internal traffic. In Storing mode it is fully stateful, and in Non-Storing mode it is fully source routed. A RPL Instance is either fully Storing or fully Non-Storing; a RPL Instance with a combination of fully Storing and Non-Storing nodes is not supported with the current specifications. External routes are advertised with non-Storing mode messaging even in a Storing mode network.
sections.plainLanguage: RPL's control messages are a kind of ICMPv6 message, with type 155. For traffic going down the tree there are two styles: routers that remember their children and forward to them, and routers that remember nothing and instead the root writes out the whole path as a list of hops.

sections.title: The Three Updates
sections.content:
Advertising external routes with Non-Storing mode signalling. Section 6.7.8 of RFC 6550 introduces the E flag, set to indicate that the 6LR generating the DAO redistributes external targets into the RPL network. An external target is a target learned through an alternate protocol, for instance a route to a prefix outside the RPL domain but reachable via a 6LR. Being outside the domain, a node reached through an external target cannot be guaranteed to ignore the RPL artifacts and cannot be expected to process the RFC 8138 compression correctly, so the artifacts should be contained in an IP-in-IP encapsulation removed by the 6LR, and any remaining compression should be expanded by the 6LR before it forwards a packet outside the domain. The document therefore updates RFC 6550 to say that advertising external targets using Non-Storing mode DAO messaging even in a Storing mode network is recommended. External routes are then not advertised within the DODAG, and all packets to an external target reach the root like normal Non-Storing mode traffic. The Non-Storing mode DAO informs the root of the address of the 6LR that injects the external route, and the root uses IP-in-IP encapsulation to that 6LR, which terminates the tunnel and forwards the original packet outside the RPL domain free of RPL artifacts. In the other direction, for traffic coming from an external target into the network, the parent that injects the traffic always encapsulates to the root, and the whole operation is transparent to intermediate routers. A RPL-unaware leaf is a special case of external target when the target is actually a host known to support a consumed Routing Header and to ignore a Hop-by-Hop Options header. A node reachable over an external route is not expected to support RFC 8138, and the 6LR that injected an external route must undo the RFC 8138 compression before forwarding over that route.

Indicating the new RPI Option Type. At the time RFC 6553 was published, leaking a Hop-by-Hop Options header in the outer IPv6 header chain could potentially impact core routers in the Internet, so it was decided to encapsulate any packet with a RPL Option using IPv6-in-IPv6 whenever it was unclear whether the packet would remain within the RPL domain. Even with the RFC 8138 compression, this yields extra bytes in a packet, meaning more energy and more bandwidth consumed, a higher chance of loss, and possibly a fragmentation at the 6LoWPAN level. RFC 8200 clarifies that nodes along a packet's delivery path are now expected to examine and process the Hop-by-Hop Options header only if explicitly configured to do so, so when the travel of a packet is unclear it becomes preferable for a source not to encapsulate, accepting that the packet may leave the RPL domain on its way to its destination. The packet should reach its destination and should not be discarded by the first node that does not recognize the RPL Option.

The document therefore updates the Option Type of the RPL Option, naming it RPI Option Type for simplicity: the two high order bits must be set to 00 and the third bit is equal to 1. The first two bits indicate that the IPv6 node must skip over this option and continue processing the header if it does not recognize the Option Type, and the third bit continues to be set to indicate that the Option Data may change en route. The rightmost five bits remain at 0x3, that is 00011. This ensures that a packet that leaves the RPL domain of a low-power network will not be discarded when it contains the RPL Option. With the new Option Type, an IPv6 intermediate node that is RPL unaware and receives a packet with a RPL Option should ignore the Hop-by-Hop RPL Option and continue processing the header. This is a significant update to RFC 6553.

Indicating the way to decompress with the new RPI Option Type. The RPI-6LoRH header provides a compressed form of the RPL RPI. A node that is decompressing this header must decompress using the RPI Option Type that is currently active, that is a choice between 0x23 and 0x63, and it will know which to use from the presence of the flag in the DODAG Configuration option. In Storing mode, the scenarios where the flow goes between RPL-unaware leaves include compression of the IPv6-in-IPv6 and RPI headers; the IPv6-in-IPv6 header must be used in this case, and it should be compressed as specified in RFC 8138.
sections.plainLanguage: Three changes. Routes that leave the network are now advertised the same way in both modes, so the root can wrap them in an extra header and the border router can strip it. The option type number changes so that a router outside the network skips the option rather than dropping the packet. And the compressed form of the option has to be expanded using whichever option type the network is currently using.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
In the data plane, a combination of RFC 6553, RFC 6554 and IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation are analyzed for a number of representative traffic flows. The use cases describe the communication between RPL-aware nodes and the root, between RPL-aware nodes and the Internet, between RPL-unaware nodes within the network, and inside the network when the final destination address resides outside it. The 24 cases are the combinations of RPL-aware leaf or RPL-unaware leaf, sending or receiving, towards the root, towards the Internet, or towards another leaf.

The document is consistent with the rule that a header cannot be inserted or removed on the fly inside an IPv6 packet that is being routed, a fundamental precept of the IPv6 architecture. As the Rank information in the RPI artifact is changed at each hop, it will typically be zero when it arrives at the DODAG root, and the root must force it to zero when passing the packet out to the Internet, so the Internet sees no SenderRank information. Despite being legal to leave the RPI artifact in place, an intermediate router that needs to add an extension header, such as RH3 or the RPL Option, must still encapsulate the packet in an additional outer IP header, with the new header placed after that outer header. An intermediate router can remove an RH3 or RPL Option only if it is placed in an encapsulating IPv6 header addressed to that router, and when doing so the whole encapsulating header must be removed, though a replacement may be added.

Both the RPL Option and the RH3 headers may be modified in very specific ways by routers on the path of the packet without needing to add and remove an encapsulating header. Both were designed with this in mind, and both are marked mutable but recoverable, so an IPsec Authentication Header can be applied across these headers but it cannot secure the values that mutate.

The reference topology has a 6LBR as the root of the global DODAG, with 6LRs below it and a mixture of RPL-aware and RPL-unaware leaves at the edges. The RPL-unaware leaves take no part in RPL at all, but use Router Advertisements, 6LoWPAN Duplicate Address Request and Confirmation, and 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery only to participate in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The use cases are a table of every combination of who is sending, who is receiving, and which direction the traffic goes: 24 of them. Two rules come out of the analysis. A router may not insert or delete a header in a packet that is already being routed, so it has to wrap the packet in an extra header instead, and that extra header must be addressed to the router that will unwrap it. The rank field inside the RPL Option is changed at each hop, so it is zero by the time the packet leaves the network.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Roughly half of the situations in the document involve leaf nodes that do not speak RPL. These fall into two categories: ones that drop a packet that has RPI or RH3 headers, and ones that continue to process a packet that has them. RFC 8200 provides rules suggesting that nodes not explicitly configured to examine Hop-by-Hop Options headers should ignore those headers and continue processing, but there may be nodes that predate RFC 8200 or are simply intolerant, and those will drop packets that still carry RPL artifacts. In general such nodes cannot be easily supported in RPL networks.

There are specific cases where it is possible to remove the RPL artifacts before forwarding a packet to a leaf host. The critical thing is that the artifacts have been inserted by the RPL root inside an IPv6-in-IPv6 header addressed to the 6LR immediately prior to the leaf, so that when the 6LR removes the IPv6-in-IPv6 header the artifacts can be removed as well. This occurs whenever traffic originates from outside the network, in the Internet cases, and Non-Storing mode is used, because in that mode the root knows the exact topology and therefore knows which 6LR is prior to the leaf. Traffic originating from the RPL root, such as when the data collection system is co-located on the root, does not require an IPv6-in-IPv6 header, as the packet is originating at the root and the root can insert the RPI and RH3 headers directly into the packet as it is formed. Such a packet is slightly smaller but can only be sent to nodes that tolerate the RPL artifacts. Because Storing mode cannot know the final path of the traffic, intolerant leaf nodes which drop packets with RPL artifacts cannot be supported in that mode.

Introducing the new RPI Option Type. During bootstrapping, the node receives the DIO with the information of the RPI Option Type, indicating the new RPI in the DODAG Configuration option flag. The DODAG root is in charge of configuring the current network with the new value through DIO messages, and determining when all the nodes have been set with the new value, and the DODAG should change to a new DODAG version. In case of rebooting, the node does not remember the RPI Option Type, so the DIO is sent with a flag indicating the new RPI Option Type.

The DODAG Configuration option is contained in a RPL DIO message, which contains a unique Destination Advertisement Trigger Sequence Number counter. The leaf nodes respond to this message with DAO messages containing the same counter, which is a normal part of RPL routing, so the RPL root knows when the updated DODAG Configuration option has been seen by all nodes. Before the migration happens, all the RPL-aware nodes should support both values. The migration procedure is triggered when the DIO is sent with the flag indicating the new RPI Option Type: the network remains at 0x63 until it is sure that the network is capable of 0x23, and then it abruptly changes. The 0x23 RPI Option allows the sending of packets to non-RPL nodes, which should ignore the option and continue processing the packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving to the new option type is a coordinated change. The root sets a flag in its DIO messages, the leaves answer with DAO messages carrying the same sequence number, and once the root has heard from everyone it knows the whole network is ready and can switch. Nodes that reboot forget which value was in use, so they wait for a DIO that says which one applies before they send anything.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The registration in the Destination Options and Hop-by-Hop Options subregistry is updated from 0x63 to 0x23: the value 0x23 is the RPL Option, and 0x63 remains registered as the RPL Option but is marked deprecated.

The DODAG Configuration Option Flags subregistry is renamed to DODAG Configuration Option Flags for MOP 0..6, and bit number 3 is registered as RPI 0x23 enable. The Mode of Operation value 7 changes from Unassigned to Reserved, in support of future work.
sections.plainLanguage: The old option number is kept in the registry but marked deprecated, a new flag bit is registered to signal that the new one is in use, and one of the mode-of-operation values is set aside for future work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations covered in RFC 6553 and RFC 6554 apply when the packets are in the RPL domain. The IPv6-in-IPv6 mechanism described here is much more limited than the general mechanism of RFC 2473. The willingness of each node in the network to decapsulate packets and forward them could be exploited by nodes to disguise the origin of an attack. While a typical low-power network may be a poor origin for attack traffic, as the networks tend to be very slow and the nodes often have very low duty cycles, given enough nodes they could still have a significant impact, particularly if the attack targets another low-power network. Some uses of RPL involve large-backbone, ISP-scale equipment with multiple 100 Gb/s interfaces.

Blocking or carefully filtering IPv6-in-IPv6 traffic entering the network makes sure that any attack must originate from compromised nodes within it. The use of network ingress filtering on egress traffic at the RPL root alerts the operator to the existence of the attack and drops the attack traffic. As the RPL network is typically numbered from a single prefix, which is itself assigned by RPL, this involves a single prefix comparison and should be trivial to configure automatically. There are some scenarios where IPv6-in-IPv6 traffic should be allowed through the RPL root, such as the IPv6-in-IPv6 mediated communications between a new pledge and the Join Registrar or Coordinator when using RFC 8555 and RFC 7430, and in that case the root does the careful filtering.

With those precautions, an attack using IPv6-in-IPv6 tunnels can only be from a node in the network to another node in the network, and could be done directly. Such an attack is meaningful only if the source addresses are fake or if the point is to amplify return traffic, and if the attack requires bidirectional communication then IPv6-in-IPv6 provides no advantage.

Whenever IPv6-in-IPv6 headers are proposed there is a concern about creating security issues. In the security considerations of RFC 2473 it was suggested that tunnel entry and exit points can be secured by securing the IPv6 path between them, but this recommendation is not practical for RPL networks. RFC 5406 gives guidance on what additional details are needed to use IPsec, and while the use of Encapsulating Security Payload would prevent source address forgeries, using it with the RFC 8138 compression would require compression to occur before encryption, because that compression is lossy. The major issue is establishing enough trust for IKEv2 to be used, which would require a system of certificates in every node, including Internet nodes that might need to communicate with the network, so using IPsec requires a global public key infrastructure in the general case. More significantly, the use of IPsec tunnels to protect the IPv6-in-IPv6 headers would, in the general case, scale with the square of the number of nodes, which is a lot of resources for constrained nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapping mechanism is the risk: a node that is willing to open and forward wrapped packets could be used to disguise where an attack came from. The mitigation is to filter wrapped traffic at the border of the network and to check the source addresses of what leaves. Protecting the wrapper with IPsec is possible in principle but needs a public key infrastructure and scales badly on small devices, so it is not what the document recommends.

viz.caption: The three RPL artifacts on the data plane

items.title: RPL Option
items.text: Carries the RPL Packet Information in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options header, including the RPLInstanceID used to spot loops.

items.title: RPL Source Route Header
items.text: An IPv6 extension header that lists the hops to follow, used to deliver datagrams within a RPL domain, particularly in Non-Storing mode.

items.title: IPv6-in-IPv6
items.text: An extra outer IPv6 header, used when a router has to add or remove an extension header in a packet that is already being routed.

viz.caption: The new RPI Option Type byte, 0x23

fields.name: act
fields.desc: Set to 00, so a node that does not recognize the option skips it and continues.

fields.name: chg
fields.desc: Set to 1, indicating that the Option Data may change on route.

fields.name: rest
fields.desc: The remaining option type bits, unchanged from the old value.

viz.caption: The two RPI Option Type values

items.label: Current
items.desc: The act bits are 00, so an unrecognised node skips the option and keeps processing the packet.

items.label: Deprecated
items.desc: The act bits are 01, so an unrecognised node discards the packet.
